newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH Q1 GDP GROWTH SURPRISES, BUT CLOUDS LOOM.
newsitem.headline: CZECH Q1 GDP GROWTH SURPRISES, BUT CLOUDS LOOM.

text.p: The Czech economy showed better-than-expected first quarter growth, though analyst reaction was muted since the data showed strong household demand despite flat retail sales and a sharp rise in inventories.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) on Thursday released figures showing real gross domestic product (GDP) for the first three months of the year rose 1.5 percent, year-on-year.

Analysts surveyed in a Reuters poll on Wednesday said that given earlier data showing a contraction in retails sales, industrial and construction output for the quarter, and a lack of investment over the period, year-on-year GDP growth should be between 0.0-0.5 percent.
"If you look at the drivers of the (GDP) increase it's mainly household consumption," said Radek Vavra of Citibank.
"(But)...in all three months of the first quarter the retail sales have been reported as flat. I'm not sure where the household consumption came from if not from retail sales."

The CSU said in a statement that overall economic output in crown terms for the first quarter totalled 268.9 billion crowns, up slightly from 264.9 billion for the same period in 1996 when GDP growth was 4.6 percent.

The statement added household consumption remained at the heart of economic growth, rising 5.4 percent and accounting for some 145.7 billion crowns. Public sector consumption, meanwhile, contracted by 1.1 percent, at 62.2 billion crowns.
It also said inventories rose 43.7 percent year-on-year, a statistic that some economists said hid the real truth about the economy.

Jiri Krovak, chief economist at WoodCommerz said that if you factored out the 22.7 billion crowns in 1997 first quarter adjusted inventories compared with the 15.8 billion crowns in 1996, the quarterly year-on-year GDP change would be a more than one percent contraction instead of 1.5 percent growth.
Krovak said he had revised his full-year GDP prognosis to two percent growth from an earlier four percent.

Other analysts dampened any optimism that the economy was on the road to recovery, noting that high interest rates used to keep the crown stable will have a strong negative effect on economic growth in the second and third quarters.
"The effect of rates has yet to be seen. They are going to really choke growth, especially if they last much longer," said one Frankfurt-based economist.

At the end of May a crown crisis caused by a wave of short-selling forced the central bank to raise its discount rate to 13 percent from 10.5 percent and the Lombard rate to 50 percent from 14 percent.

Eventually the CNB even cut off access to the Lombard lending facility as well as reaching an agreement with some local banks on cutting off non-resident access to the local money market to restrain availability of crowns.

The central bank has removed the Lombard and money market restrictions recently, but has not touched either of its key rates. CNB officials have said the top priority remains crown stability, even at the cost of short-term economic growth.
Nonetheless, the crown reacted positively to the news, firming to 18.545 against the mark versus 18.646 before figures were released.

"I expect some small appreciation of the Czech crown but nothing dramatic...It's a surprise because personally we expected (GDP growth) between zero and one percent," said Tomas Becvar, a trader at Komercni Banka.

The economy was given a further dose of positive economic news by the release of key M2 money data, which showed the downtrend in money supply growth had continued in April, easing to 5.3 percent, year-on-year growth from 6.3 percent the previous month.
The CNB figures include the influence of domestic deposits connected to the $1.32 billion equity expansion of SPT Telecom a.s. in the summer of 1995.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
